entries.sense: Bond of shared life and close association between persons, whether among believers or between believers and God, Christ or the Spirit. This is the relational sense only; participation in a thing and concrete generosity are covered by alternates.

alternates.when: The word denotes joint engagement in a shared undertaking or working agreement, not the relationship as such: Gal 2:9 (right hand of partnership), Phil 1:5 (partnership in the good news), Phlm 6 (partnership of your faith, linked to 'partner' in v. 17).

alternates.rendering: sharing in / a sharing in / participation in
alternates.when: The word is followed by a genitive of the thing shared in and the sense is taking part in it: 1 Cor 10:16 (blood and body of Christ), Phil 3:10 (his sufferings), 2 Cor 8:4 (the service to the holy ones). This does not apply to the genitive 'of the Spirit' in 2 Cor 13:13 and Phil 2:1, which take the default 'fellowship of the Spirit' so that the open genitive is kept and the two verses match.

alternates.rendering: sharing / contribution / share / to share / share something
alternates.when: The word denotes concrete generosity, the act of sharing goods or money with others: Rom 15:26, 2 Cor 9:13, Heb 13:16. A verbal recast such as 'to share' is acceptable where English needs it.

entries.traditional: fellowship (also 'communion' in 1 Cor 10:16 and 2 Cor 13:13; 'contribution' in Rom 15:26)
entries.rationale: The Greek word means having something in common, and it covered business partnerships and marriage as well as friendship. For the bond between persons, 'fellowship' is still the English word that best holds both the relationship and the shared life, and a lexicographer would list it. 'Partnership' sounds commercial and implies equals when used of the Father or the Son, so it is kept for the passages where a joint undertaking is in view. A note can warn that the word is stronger than modern 'fellowship' may suggest.
entries.standard_view: Most translations (KJV, NASB, ESV, NIV, NRSV) use 'fellowship' for the relational sense in Acts 2:42, 1 Cor 1:9, 2 Cor 6:14, Gal 2:9 and 1 John 1. They use 'participation', 'sharing' or 'communion' in 1 Cor 10:16 and Phil 3:10, 'contribution' or 'sharing' in Rom 15:26, 2 Cor 9:13 and Heb 13:16, and often 'partnership' in Phil 1:5. They divide over the Spirit phrases: 2 Cor 13:13 is usually 'fellowship' or 'communion of the Holy Spirit', while Phil 2:1 is often 'participation in' or 'sharing in the Spirit', and many scholars favour the participation reading in both. Acts 2:42 is disputed between the community's bond in general and the sharing of goods specifically, and Phlm 6 is widely regarded as obscure. Most versions keep 'fellowship' in Gal 2:9, so 'partnership' there is an editorial departure, though lexically well supported.

entries.sense: one who robs with violence, typically armed and often in a gang; a brigand or highwayman, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth
entries.traditional: robber, with thief in the KJV in several places
entries.rationale: Greek distinguishes this word from the one for a thief who steals by stealth; this one denotes an armed, violent plunderer such as a highwayman or brigand. 'Robber' is not wrong, but in modern English it can suggest a burglar or mugger, and the KJV's 'thief' blurs the distinction altogether. 'Bandit' keeps the element of violence and outlawry, fits every New Testament occurrence, and leaves room for the insurgent overtone some see in the Passion narratives without asserting it. A single rendering also keeps the word recognisably the same across the temple saying, the arrest, the crucifixion and Barabbas.
entries.standard_view: Standard lexicons gloss the word as robber, highwayman or bandit, and note that it was also applied to insurrectionists, as in Josephus. Most modern translations (ESV, NASB, NIV in most places) use 'robber'; the NRSV uses 'bandit' in many of these verses. Some versions render it 'rebel', 'revolutionary' or 'insurrectionist' for the men crucified with Jesus, at the arrest scene, or for Barabbas; that reading is possible but not certain. The KJV's 'thieves' in the temple saying and the crucifixion is generally regarded as imprecise.

entries.sense: figurative: something that trips a person up or ensnares them, causing a fall into sin, unbelief or ruin; also a person or thing that acts as such an obstacle

alternates.rendering: that makes people fall / rock that makes people fall
alternates.when: In the quoted phrase πέτρα σκανδάλου from Isaiah 8:14 (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8), where the paired λίθος προσκόμματος already takes the stumbling wording. Use the same rendering in both places.

Where σκάνδαλον stands beside πρόσκομμα and πρόσκομμα has already been rendered "stumbling block" (Romans 14:13). Not in Romans 11:9, where "snare" and "trap" are taken by παγίς and θήρα and σκάνδαλον keeps the default.

alternates.rendering: cause for stumbling / that causes stumbling / everything that causes stumbling
alternates.when: Where "stumbling block" is awkward in English: the collective πάντα τὰ σκάνδαλα in Matthew 13:41, which may include persons, and the abstract "there is no σκάνδαλον in him" in 1 John 2:10.

entries.traditional: offence (KJV); stumbling block in most modern versions
entries.rationale: In the Septuagint and the New Testament the word means a trap or an obstacle that makes someone fall, and figuratively whatever leads a person into sin or ruin. The older "offence" now suggests hurt feelings, and "hindrance" is too mild. "Stumbling block" is established English, conveys the image accurately, and is already what the run uses most often.
entries.standard_view: Most modern translations (NIV, NRSV, ESV, NASB) use "stumbling block" in the majority of occurrences. They vary it with "cause of stumbling", "causes of sin", "temptations to sin", "hindrance", "obstacle" or "offense" in particular verses. In the Isaiah 8:14 quotation they have "rock of offense" (ESV, NASB) or "a rock that makes them fall" (NIV, NRSV). Lexicons give "trap", "temptation to sin or enticement", and "that which causes offense or revulsion"; the last is often applied to 1 Corinthians 1:23 and Galatians 5:11, where most versions nonetheless keep "stumbling block".

entries.sense: Figurative sense only: of teaching, words, or a person's faith being sound, that is correct and uncorrupted (1-2 Timothy, Titus).

alternates.when: Figurative sense where the verb is finite or the English needs a verb, as in Titus 1:13 'so that they may be sound in the faith'.

alternates.rendering: be healthy / be well / be in good health / healthy / in good health / safe and sound
alternates.when: Literal sense of bodily health or well-being: Luke 5:31; 7:10; 15:27; 3 John 1:2. 'Safe and sound' fits only the returned son in Luke 15:27.

entries.traditional: sound, as in sound doctrine, sound words, sound in the faith
entries.rationale: The Greek verb ordinarily means to be in good health, but it was also an established way of calling opinions or speech correct and sensible. English 'sound' has the same range, from 'sound in body' and 'safe and sound' to 'sound advice', so it matches the Greek closely and does not mislead. 'Healthy teaching' is defensible but can suggest teaching that is good for you rather than teaching that is itself uncorrupted, and 'healthy words' is awkward English. 'Sound' still lets the contrast with 'sick' teachers (1 Tim 6:4) and talk that spreads like gangrene (2 Tim 2:17) come through, and a note can point out the image where it is live.
entries.standard_view: Most major English versions keep 'sound' for the teaching phrases. Some use 'healthy' or 'wholesome' in places, especially of persons in Titus 1:13 and 2:2. Standard lexicons gloss the figurative use as 'be sound, be correct'. Scholars disagree on how live the medical metaphor is: some read it as a conventional term for reasonable, correct teaching, while others stress a deliberate medical polemic against opponents pictured as diseased. The default sides with tradition but does not deny the image.

entries.sense: to come or go to see someone out of concern for their welfare; chiefly God coming to his people to act for them, and also people going to see how others are doing

alternates.when: The object is people in need (the sick, prisoners, orphans, widows) and the point is practical care rather than the act of going to see them: Matthew 25:36, 25:43; James 1:27.
Hebrews 2:6, the quotation of Psalm 8, where the verb is parallel to 'remember' and describes God's standing concern for humankind rather than a coming.
Acts 15:14, where the verb has no personal object and is completed by an infinitive ('to take a people'), so 'visit' cannot be used without adding words.
The separate sense of looking over a group in order to choose someone: Acts 6:3.

entries.rationale: In the Greek Old Testament this verb is the regular word for God 'visiting' his people to rescue or provide for them (for example Ruth 1:6), and Luke's songs echo that language. With God as subject, 'visit' still conveys a purposeful coming, the context states the help ('and worked redemption'), and the word keeps the link with the related noun 'visitation'. 'Come to help' spells out more than the verb says and cannot be used in Luke 1:78 or Acts 15:14. Where the object is the sick or destitute, 'visit' now suggests a mere call, so 'look after' is used there.
entries.standard_view: KJV, ESV, NASB and CSB keep 'visit' for God's action in Luke 1:68, 1:78 and 7:16; NIV has 'come to' or 'come to help', and NRSV has 'looked favorably on'. In Acts 15:14 versions divide between 'visited' with a supplied object, 'concerned himself', 'looked favorably' and 'intervened'. In Hebrews 2:6 most modern versions have 'care for' and some 'are concerned about'. In Matthew 25 and James 1:27 most keep 'visit', while NIV has 'look after' and NRSV 'care for' in James. Lexicons gloss the divine sense as a gracious visitation to bring help, so both 'visit' and 'come to help' are defensible and the default is an editorial choice.

entries.sense: to act as shepherd: literally to tend a flock, and figuratively to lead, care for or govern people as a shepherd does, including the royal and iron-rod uses

alternates.when: Literal herding with no object expressed, where English needs the object supplied, as in Luke 17:7.

entries.traditional: feed or rule in the King James tradition; shepherd or tend in most modern versions, but still rule in the iron-rod verses of Revelation
entries.rationale: The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for a shepherd and means to do a shepherd's work. A first-century reader heard that image even where the subject is a king or church leader, because shepherd was a standing picture for a ruler in the Greek Old Testament. "Feed" is too narrow and "rule" drops the image, while "shepherd" is still clear English. Using it throughout also lets the reader see that Revelation uses the same verb for the Lamb's care in 7:17 and for the iron rod in 2:27, 12:5 and 19:15.
entries.standard_view: Most modern translations use "shepherd" or "tend" for the pastoral passages (John 21:16, Acts 20:28, 1 Peter 5:2) and "shepherd" in Matthew 2:6 and Revelation 7:17. In Revelation 2:27, 12:5 and 19:15 nearly all have "rule", and standard lexicons list these verses under a sense of ruling with destructive effect. Some scholars argue that there, following the Greek form of Psalm 2:9, the verb is closer to "crush" or "devastate". A minority of literal versions keep "shepherd" in those verses. In Jude 1:12 many versions have "feeding themselves" or "caring only for themselves".

entries.sense: to slaughter: to butcher an animal, especially for sacrifice, and by extension to kill a person violently and bloodily
entries.rationale: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for butchering an animal, used in the Septuagint for sacrificial slaughter and also for brutal killing of people; it is not the common word for 'kill'. 'Slain' is now archaic and solemn and loses that bluntness, while 'kill' or 'murder' loses the butchery image that ties the Lamb, the martyrs and Cain's victim together. Using 'slaughter' everywhere, including Revelation 13:3, also lets the reader see that the beast's wounded head is described with the same word as the Lamb.
entries.standard_view: Standard lexicons gloss the verb as 'slaughter', and also 'murder' for violent killing of persons. Most English versions use 'slain' for the Lamb and the martyrs in Revelation, though some modern versions use 'slaughtered' there. In 1 John 3:12 most have 'murdered', 'killed' or 'slew'. In Revelation 13:3 most paraphrase as 'a mortal wound', 'wounded to death' or 'fatal wound' rather than keeping the verb.

entries.sense: As a noun: a specialist in interpreting the Jewish Law (the Gospel occurrences). The adjective use in Titus 3:9 and the reference to Zenas in Titus 3:13 are covered by alternates.

alternates.when: Titus 3:13, of Zenas. He has a Greek name and appears outside a Palestinian setting, so he may be a jurist in Roman or Greek law rather than a Torah specialist. The text does not settle which, and the general word 'lawyer' leaves it open.

alternates.rendering: over the law / about the law / legal
alternates.when: Adjective use in Titus 3:9 (μάχας νομικάς), describing disputes concerned with the law.

entries.rationale: In the Gospels the word names men learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with those called scribes. To a modern reader 'lawyer' suggests an attorney representing clients in court, which misleads. 'Expert in the law' says what a first-century reader would have understood, and the run already uses it throughout the Gospels. The lowercase 'law' is fixed here only for consistency within the phrase.
entries.standard_view: Lexicons gloss the noun as one learned in the law, a legal expert, and in the Gospels specifically an expert in the Mosaic law. The KJV, RSV, NRSV, ESV and NASB keep 'lawyer'. The NIV, NET and CSB use 'expert in the law' or something close to it. For Zenas in Titus 3:13 nearly all versions have 'lawyer', and commentators are divided on whether he was a Roman jurist or a Jewish legal expert.

entries.sense: person afflicted with the ritually defiling scaly skin condition of Leviticus 13-14 (the only sense in the New Testament)

alternates.rendering: man with a skin disease / men with a skin disease
alternates.when: The context identifies the sufferer as a man or men, as with the individual in Matthew 8:2 and Mark 1:40 and the ten men of Luke 17:12, where the Greek adds the word for men.

alternates.rendering: those with skin disease / people with skin disease / those with a skin disease / people with a skin disease
alternates.when: Plural used of the afflicted as a class, as in Matthew 10:8, 11:5, Luke 4:27 and 7:22.

Only in the fixed byname Simon the leper at Matthew 26:6 and Mark 14:3, where the word works as an identifying nickname and not as a description of his present condition. A note should explain the term.

entries.rationale: In the Septuagint and in first-century Jewish usage this word names someone with the condition regulated in Leviticus 13-14: a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why they are 'cleansed' and not simply healed. 'Leper' and 'leprosy' today mean Hansen's disease, which is narrower than the Greek term and may not even be included in it, so the traditional word misleads a modern reader about what is described. 'Skin disease' is the description standard lexicons give, and the run already favours it. The familiar byname of Simon is kept because it identifies him rather than diagnoses him.
entries.standard_view: Most major translations (KJV, ESV, NRSV, NET) keep 'leper', and NIV and CSB use 'person with leprosy', usually with a footnote saying the term covers various skin diseases. A minority, such as the CEB and the HCSB ('serious skin disease'), put that in the text. Scholars widely agree the biblical term is broader than modern leprosy. The disagreement is whether to keep the familiar word with a note, since 'skin disease' can understate the severity and social exclusion involved.

entries.sense: A course of action one has committed to, such as a plan, project or firm stand. This is the sense at 2 Corinthians 9:4, 11:17 and Hebrews 3:14, where tradition has 'confidence'. It is not the 'underlying reality' sense of Hebrews 1:3 and 11:1.

alternates.when: Hebrews 3:14, where the word names the commitment the readers began with and must hold firm to the end; 'undertaking' is too project-like there.
Hebrews 1:3, where the word means God's essential nature or actual being, of which the Son is the exact imprint.
Hebrews 11:1, where faith is called the ὑπόστασις of things hoped for. This is the objective sense of underlying reality or what gives something substance, paired with 'proof' for ἔλεγχος.

entries.traditional: confidence at 2 Corinthians 9:4, 11:17 and Hebrews 3:14; substance or assurance at Hebrews 11:1; person, nature or being at Hebrews 1:3
entries.rationale: In the usage of the period the word normally refers to something objective: what underlies or stands firm, an underlying reality, or a plan or project one has taken on. Lexicographers have questioned whether the inner feeling 'confidence' is securely attested for it. 'Undertaking' suits Paul's collection project and his project of boasting. At Hebrews 3:14 the related use for a firm stand gives 'resolve', which fits the call to hold fast. This is an editorial choice in a disputed area, and 'confidence' remains defensible.
entries.standard_view: Most English versions (KJV, ESV, NIV and others) render 'confidence', 'confident' or 'conviction' at 2 Corinthians 9:4, 11:17 and Hebrews 3:14. The NRSV has 'undertaking' at 2 Corinthians 9:4 but 'confidence' at the other two. At Hebrews 11:1 most modern versions have 'assurance' or 'confidence' (KJV 'substance'), though some have 'reality', and many commentators favour an objective sense. At Hebrews 1:3 'being' or 'nature' is standard (KJV 'person'). The standard modern lexicon and specialist word studies argue against 'confidence' and for 'plan, undertaking', 'situation' or 'reality'. Scholarship is divided, and the traditional rendering is still widely defended.

entries.sense: a first payment that secures a transaction and commits the payer to the rest; used figuratively of the Spirit given to believers
entries.rationale: In the commercial Greek of the period the word meant money paid in advance that both forms part of the full payment and binds the payer to complete it. "Earnest" in this sense is no longer understood by modern readers, and "guarantee" or "pledge" conveys the assurance but loses the idea that part of the thing itself has already been handed over. "Down payment" is ordinary modern English that keeps both ideas, and standard lexicons list it among the glosses.
entries.standard_view: The KJV has "earnest". Modern versions divide: ESV and NKJV use "guarantee", NASB "pledge", NIV "deposit" with "guaranteeing" added, NRSV "first installment" in 2 Corinthians and "pledge" in Ephesians, and CSB and NET "down payment". Scholars agree it is a commercial loanword from Semitic for earnest money or a deposit; in the Septuagint of Genesis 38 it is a pledge that is later returned, so some prefer "pledge", but the part-payment sense is the common commercial one and fits Paul's use of the Spirit as a first share of what is to come.

loanword_test: A Greek term is left untranslated only if all three hold: it functions as a title or proper name; every English candidate actively misleads a modern reader, rather than merely falling short; and it occurs in few enough places that the text stays English. Logos (John 1), Gehenna and Hades pass. Ordinary vocabulary such as pneuma and sarx does not.
